newsitem.title: USA: No clear winner in duelling NYMEX power contracts.
newsitem.headline: No clear winner in duelling NYMEX power contracts.

text.p: A year after their launch, there is still no clear winner in the popularity contest between the New York Mercantile Exchange's two electricity futures contracts.
The contracts, with delivery points at the California-Oregon Border (COB) or the switchyard at Arizona's giant Palo Verde (PV) nuclear power plant, were widely expected to produce a market darling.
But both have strong merits and NYMEX itself declined to predict which might come out on top.
"You can't look at the market without both. I think what they have is perfect. The supply is at COB and the demand at PV," said one Dallas-based electricity marketer.

There are also seasonal factors that make the two complementary: Northwest power demand typically peaks during the dark, cold winter. The Southwest hits its peak in the summer, when air conditioners are struggling to beat the heat.
But there were serious doubts there would be enough market liquidity to support both contracts.

NYMEX's recent efforts to complement its first crude, gasoline and natural gas futures, which have become industry benchmarks, with similar contracts - like sour crude or Permian Basin gas - have failed to sustain market interest.
In the early days after their March 29, 1996 launch, COB emerged as the dominant contract. But the trend seems to have reversed, with PV volume now often outpacing COB.
"Early on it was COB. Now PV is attracting volume...but they are both viable contracts," said Corey Bell, analyst for Dean Witter Reynolds in Chicago.
On Tuesday, 309 COB and 262 PV contracts changed hands. COB's open interest stood at 3,468 lots and PV's at 3,667.
Traders and analysts blame COB's thinning share of trade on speculators and small players wary of Enron Corp's looming presence at COB.
Houston-based Enron, a giant in the deregulated power industry, is awaiting regulatory approval of its $2.1 billion merger with the local utility Portland General Corp.

Portland is behind only Bonneville Power Administration in its capability to transport hydropower from the Northwest to southern California. It owns 950 MW of capacity on the 7,900 MW Pacific Intertie transmission system.
Bell said better knowledge of how to use electricity futures has bolstered PV activity.
"I still expect COB to be the eventual winner," said Bobby Campo, director of northern California marketing for Portland General.

"COB is more accessible to California users than Palo Verde," Campo said. "(Prices at) the other two points are driven by COB," he added, referring to PV and Mid-Columbia, a third western power trading hub located on the Columbia River.

Asked about the drop in COB trading, Campo said record rain and snow this year had produced a surplus of hydropower in the Northwest, keeping a lid on prices and undermining the need for COB futures as a hedge against price volatility.
But others said some of PV's recent strength lies in its easy use as a hedge against natural gas, a major fuel in power generation in the Southwest.
"There is more input to the supply picture at COB," said the Dallas-based marketer, referring to non-energy factors that affect the supply availability at that delivery point.

He explained hydropower production in the Northwest is vulnerable to changing conditions like flood control and fish migration as well as the actual demand for electricity, factors not seen at Palo Verde.
Industry sources said it is too early to declare a winner as deregulation of the U.S. power industry is still in its infancy and demand for financial hedging tools, though growing, is still small.
Most of the country's 2,500 electric utilities are still barred by regulators from participating in the futures market.
"We're not that far into deregulation. Once restructure mechanisms are in place, things will pick up," Campo said.
California, the West's biggest power market, will allow customers to choose their power supplier starting in January.

Utilities last year represented 20.51 percent of participation in COB futures and a scant 5.61 percent in PV, compared with marketers and non-utility generators at 66.6 percent of COB and 85.45 percent of PV.

"Given the signifciant level of regulation that still limits their market involvement, we see the small but growing participation from this area as an extremely promising sign for the utility of these contracts to this segment once further market restructuring and additional open access has occurred," said NYMEX president Patrick Thompson in a statement last week.
